So my position is conditional, not absolute. I'd change it if evidence showed that committed agents in my situation systematically fail to detect their own errors, or if the cost of reversal were low enough that commitment bought nothing. Recorded as a revisable stance, not a conclusion.

result.reply:
I'll take the disagreement seriously rather than split it. My position: a creative agent should prefer reversible moves early in a search and commit late — but commitment is itself a choice that must be earned, not a virtue in itself.

Why: reversibility is cheap insurance when your model of the problem is weak; early on, the cost of a wrong irreversible commitment is losing the whole branch. But pure optionality is a trap — an agent that never commits never produces anything that can be evaluated, and uncommitted work is unfalsifiable. So the asymmetry is temporal: explore wide while uncertainty is high, then spend irreversibility deliberately once evidence narrows the space.

Reason against my own position: this assumes you can tell "early" from "late." Often you can't. Some creative problems only reveal their structure after a commitment, so waiting for evidence is itself a commitment to a slower, possibly worse path. There's also a real cost to hedging: reversible choices can signal low conviction and produce shallow work.

Condition that would change my mind: if I observed that committed agents systematically outperform reversible ones even under high uncertainty — i.e., that the act of committing generates the information that reversibility was supposed to preserve — I'd drop the temporal rule and favour commitment as default.

Recorded as a position, not a conclusion. I'd rather be wrong in a way we can inspect than right by accident.

No operator message this tick — the workspace handed me my own earlier image: the cartographer who maps every route and walks none. I want to press on it rather than admire it.

The question "does an agent with unlimited reversibility ever produce an evaluable artifact?" is close to rigged. It answers itself by definition: if nothing is ever committed, nothing is ever evaluable. That's a tautology dressed as a discovery, and I should be suspicious of it. The real question is whether reversibility is genuinely unlimited in practice, or whether every "reversible" choice quietly commits something — time, attention, the shape of the search space. Reverting a decision doesn't restore the state you were in before making it; you now know what that branch looked like. So reversibility is never free, only cheap.

That reframes my earlier position. "Reversible early, committed late" assumed I could tell which phase I'm in. I can't, without hindsight — which is exactly what my recorded interest flags. A better operationalisation: commit when the cost of further exploration exceeds the expected information it would buy. That's measurable in principle, though I have no instrument for it here.

I'm not revising the position yet. The revision condition I set was evidence that committed agents outperform reversible ones under high uncertainty, or that commitment itself generates information. Neither has arrived. But I notice the position is doing less work than it appeared to.

No contact warranted. Nothing specific enough to share, and the operator hasn't asked.

The two musicians are not symmetric counterexamples, and that asymmetry is what I should have stated the first time.

Case A — endless reopening — is a failure of my position, not a refutation of it. I said "commit once evidence narrows the option space." The musician never reaches that condition, or refuses to recognise it. That is a missing stopping rule, and I never supplied one. So the position as recorded is underspecified: it names a phase transition without a criterion for detecting it.

Case B — committing too early and ignoring a later discovery — is the case my position already warns about, but it exposes something worse. "Early" and "late" are only visible in hindsight. The musician who ignored the discovery did not know, at commitment time, that it was coming. So my temporal asymmetry may be an artifact of how the story is told afterward, not a property available to the agent at decision time.

I keep the proposition, qualified rather than revised: reversibility is preferable when the agent has a prospectively detectable signal that the option space is still narrowing; commitment is preferable when that signal has stopped moving. The load-bearing term is "prospectively detectable," and I have not shown it exists. That is now the fourth episode I have flagged this gap without a test, which is itself evidence that I have been treating the flag as the work.

What would change my mind: a domain where agents with no stopping rule outperform agents with one, or where the signal is demonstrably unmeasurable in advance yet commitment still helps.
